meta.method: Independent verification of the editor's pass on the north-america tour (editor-brief.md, Verifier's brief). For every id in meta.edited_ids: old and new title/statement compared against the editor's saved copy, every fact in the new text checked in the cited pages (etl.research.source from the fetch cache) in context past the quote, transitions checked against the sources, computed figures against notes, confidence and standing checked, then the whole tour read in stop order. verify_quotes: missing 0 on both catalogues; voice: no hit on an edited card; copying: no 15-word run, nothing over 80 words; no id/date/place/kind/qid/participants field changed; no unlisted change. Convention: partially-verified means the fix should be applied; verified with a fix means the fix is optional, for flow or clarity, and the card is sound as it stands. A fix that adds a fact names the verbatim quote to add to the citations.

na-e-042.fix: At the army's command Black Kettle settled his people, around 750 Cheyenne and Arapaho, at Big Sandy Creek. On 29 November 1864 Colonel John Chivington's Colorado troops attacked; Captain Silas Soule and Lieutenant Joseph Cramer told their men to hold fire. Chivington claimed 500 to 600 warriors killed, but estimates of the dead run from about 70 to 230, mostly women, children and the elderly. A congressional committee later said it could hardly find fitting terms to describe his conduct.

Optional fix adds one line from the ND Studies page; add the quote 'Red Cloud, an Oglala Lakota, declared that he would continue to make war on travelers and Army posts until the government closed the road and removed the Army.' (ndstudies.gov/gr8/node/137). It drops 'for exclusive Sioux use' and 'reserved unceded hunting lands' to stay at 80 words. Optional fix applied exactly as proposed.
na-e-045.fix: Red Cloud's Lakota had fought the army over the Bozeman Trail forts on Sioux treaty land. The treaty signed from 29 April 1868 by Lakota, Yanktonai, Santee and Arapaho leaders ended that war: it recognized the Black Hills as part of the Great Sioux Reservation, and the government promised to close the trail and its forts. No later cession would be valid unless three-fourths of adult Sioux men signed. In 1874 Custer's expedition found gold there, and miners moved in.

na-e-067.fix: Fifteen years after Red River, Louis Riel led a second rising, the North-West Resistance or Rebellion, decided at Batoche, the capital of his Provisional Government of Saskatchewan. From 9 to 12 May 1885 General Frederick Middleton's 916 regulars and militia attacked its trenches and rifle pits, held under Gabriel Dumont, until greater numbers and firepower overwhelmed the Métis. Middleton reported 51 Métis dead, a priest 16, and historians commonly accept 12. Riel surrendered on 15 May, and his government collapsed.

na-e-075.note: Facts verified: 4 August 1701, Callière, 1,300 from 39 nations, French brokering, all-out war not returning, the Odawa attack and the Huron club. Flow: the Beaver Wars are never explained on the tour. Optional fix; add the quotes 'The Beaver Wars saw the Hurons and Algonquins, supported by the French, pitted against the Haudenosaunee of the powerful League of Five Nations' and 'Control over the fur trade became a high-stakes game among the Native American tribes' (Great_Peace_of_Montreal). It drops 'near a French fort' to stay at 80 words. Optional fix applied exactly as proposed.
na-e-075.fix: In the north, the Beaver Wars, the fight over the fur trade between the Haudenosaunee and the French with their Huron and Algonquin allies, ended on 4 August 1701, when Louis-Hector de Callière, governor of New France, and 1,300 representatives of 39 Indigenous nations signed a peace at Montreal. All-out war did not return, though within three years Odawa warriors attacked a Haudenosaunee village near present-day Kingston and planted a Huron club on a dead warrior to provoke new fighting.

na-e-183.note: Facts verified in the NPS page. One date compression: the page says the leaders spoke with Twisted Hair after the expedition reunited on 22 September, not on that day. Fix restores 'after', trimming elsewhere to stay under 80 words. Fix applied exactly as proposed.
na-e-183.fix: In mid-September 1805, crossing the Bitterroots, William Clark went ahead with a few hunters for food and came out on Weippe Prairie, where the Nez Perce gathered in summer for roots, berries and game. They met three frightened boys hiding in the grass and gave them small presents. The Nez Perce, nervous of these strangers, accepted them, and after the expedition reunited on 22 September its leaders traded gifts and passed the pipe with the head man Twisted Hair.

Dropping the speech is defensible; the owner may want 'I will fight no more forever' back, since it is in the NPS page. Owner's request: restore 'I will fight no more forever', worded as what is recorded. The reworded card went to a second independent verifier, which corrected 'go home' to 'return to Idaho' and '431' to 'over 400' and verified the rest; its wording was applied exactly.
na-e-187.fix: War in Idaho sent about 800 Nez Perce fleeing the US Army in summer 1877. From 30 September Colonel Nelson Miles besieged them forty miles short of Canada, and cannon fire targeted the families' shelters. On 5 October, told they would return to Idaho, Joseph surrendered; the words recorded as his, in translation, end 'I will fight no more forever'. The promise was overruled, and those who surrendered or were captured, over 400, were sent to Kansas and Indian Territory.

na-e-203.note: Facts verified: Montana Trail attack as the 'final catalyst', 29 January 1863, Bear Hunter's winter camp, 21 soldiers, 156 (Warner) to 493 (Jasperson, a Danish immigrant: 'settler' is fair), 'some sources' on the largest mass murder. Framing: the card now opens with the Shoshone attack as the sole cause of a massacre, which the page itself presents as the last of a chain beginning with settlers taking over Cache Valley's food sources and Shoshone starvation; the old card had no cause at all. Fix adds the background in the page's own terms; add the quote 'the settlers were consuming significant food resources and taking over areas that pushed the Shoshone increasingly into areas of marginal food production' (Bear_River_Massacre). 78 words. Fix applied exactly as proposed.
na-e-203.fix: Settlers had taken over Cache Valley's food sources; the final catalyst for Colonel Patrick Connor's expedition was a Shoshone attack on miners on the Montana Trail. On 29 January 1863 his California Volunteers struck Bear Hunter's winter encampment. Some 21 soldiers died. Estimates of the Shoshone dead run from 156, from the chief Sagwitch's son, to 493, counted by a settler among the bodies. Some call it the largest mass murder of Native Americans by the US military.
